title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Pursuing Funding in the Public and Private Sectors: Opportunities and Challenges
description:
Securing funding is one of the most consequential — and least openly discussed — dimensions of a research career. For scholars whose work centers social inequality and structurally marginalized communities, pursuing funding carries unique political and institutional complexities. This workshop engages those realities directly. Participants will examine how funding priorities are shaped, how research agendas can be both advanced and constrained by funders, and how to build a diversified, sustainable funding strategy across sectors — without losing sight of their scholarly mission or community commitments.

In this workshop, Dr. Rashawn Ray, whose funding portfolio spans federal agencies, private foundations, and philanthropic institutions, will demystify the landscape of public and private research support. Through a combination of presentations, case discussions, and small-group work, participants will leave with:

A working knowledge of the public funding landscape. An understanding of how federal agencies like the National Science Foundation fund social science research, including how to identify the right programs, align research questions with agency priorities, and navigate the review process.Familiarity with private and philanthropic funding. Insight into how foundations such as the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and Russell Sage Foundation operate, what differentiates their funding logic from federal agencies, and how to position applied scholarship for philanthropic support.Awareness of the structural dynamics of funding. A candid examination of how funding opportunities are not equally distributed and strategies for navigating and challenging those inequities.A personalized funding roadmap. A draft funding strategy tailored to each participant’s research agenda, career stage, and institutional context, with identified targets across both public and private sectors.Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: AI Assisted Surveys
description:
This course will be held online only over 3 days (September 14, 16, and 18). Attendance is required as it will not be recorded.

This 6-hour course provides training on how AI can assist a survey project from beginning to the end.

We will focus on each step of the research process (Callegaro and Yang, 2025)

PlanningExecutionActivationIn the planning phase there are two sub phases
1) Ideate and define

AI can be an idea helper and assist on generating research ideas starting from previously knowledgeA literature review can definitely be assisted by AI and there are specific tools available for that2) Design and plan

The design stage is where AI can assist in producing design brief, analysis plan and map the concepts that are going to be measured using the questionnaireThe execution phase consists of
3) Data wizard

Here AI has been used to help drafting and pretesting the questionnaire, help writing survey material such as survey invitation and confidentiality assurances.4) Analysis copilot

Once the data collection is under way, AI can assist in automating, and writing statistical code to analyze the dataset (stat code assistant). It can also be used as  theme discovery, for coding of open ended answers and data visualization.The activation phase consists of:
5) Insight partner

Help summarize findings, generate reports, help review the final deliverables such as a research report or a complete academic paper6) Storytelling aid

Develop presentation materials, create multi-media artifacts, generated blog post for different platforms, generate images based on content from the researchOrganizational Structure of the Course 
The course will be taught in a workshop style where the lectures will be using presentation slides as a roadmap. After each concept has been introduced and discussed, the participants will be invited to work on brief hands on exercises with different LLMs such as Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and ChatGPT

Participants will be strongly encouraged to ask questions during lectures, especially on how the content relates to their own research.

Learning objectives
By the end of the course, you will:

Learn how to prompt LLMs for survey research help and assistanceLearn how to evaluate the quality of LLMs outputsStrengths and challenges of different LLMs toolsWhere LLMs are not necessaryEthical usage of LLMs/AI ToolsRecent debate of using LLMs to produce research and write academic papersRegistration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.
source: NC State African American Cultural Center

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

description:
Learn more about the history of the nation’s first public university by attending a Carolina History Tour. The Carolina History Tours cover more than 200 years of the history of UNC-Chapel Hill, including the establishment of the university in the 18th century, the history of campus landmarks including the Old Well, Davie Poplar, and Unsung Founders Memorial, the push to open enrollment to all North Carolinians, and the growth of the school in the 20th and 21st centuries. Tours will begin at the Old Well and finish at Wilson Library. Most tours last a little over an hour. 

Led by staff from the Wilson Special Collections Library, these tours are part of the University Library’s commitment to collecting, preserving, and sharing the history of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

title: Open Studio: Glass & Other
location: Fusion Gallery, 321 W Main St, Durham, 27701, United States
description:
Open Studio Day Pass
Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM. 
Use our studio space and tools or bring your own project to work on—perfect for artists who don’t have a home studio or simply want dedicated time and space to make. Personal cubbies are also available to store works-in-progress between visits. 
Online registration or sign-up via email is required before coming in. Drop-ins are not permitted at this time. If you’d like to come in at a time you don’t see available online, email us at info@fusionnc.com. 
How Open Studio Works
Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction. You should already have the skills needed to safely work in your chosen medium. It’s also a great opportunity to finish projects started during a Fusion class. 
Your Day Pass includes access to our shared workspace, tools, equipment, and currently available non-consumable materials. Consumable and specialty materials are charged separately based on usage. 
Stained & Fused Glass
Prior stained or fused glass experience is required to use our glass tools. Taking a basics or beginner class at Fusion is recommended, but previous instruction at Carolina Stained Glass or Say It With Glass is also accepted. 
• Glass, solder, foil, and frit: $35/lb
• Bringing your own stained glass? Foil and solder use: $6
• Paper stained glass patterns: Free
• Vinyl-cut patterns: $3 each
• An assortment of stained glass patterns is available for studio use
• Kiln firings are handled by Fusion staff only 
Silver Clay
Prior silver clay experience is required to use silver clay tools. Taking a beginner class at Fusion is recommended before using the studio independently. 
• Silver clay: $7/gram prior to firing
• Firing of your completed piece is included and will be completed at the convenience of Fusion studio staff
• Guests may not fire their own pieces without prior authorization from Fusion’s owners 
Drawing & Painting
No prior class or experience is required for drawing or painting. Your Open Studio fee includes access to currently available shared drawing and painting materials. 
Please Note
• Day Pass access is valid 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected date only
• Online or email registration is required before arriving—no walk-ins
• Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction
• Some specialty tools, equipment, or processes may require prior approval or demonstrated experience
• Guests are responsible for cleaning their workspace and helping maintain a respectful shared environment
• Misuse of the space, tools, or equipment or failure to follow studio guidelines may result in removal from the studio without refund

title: Bike MS 2026 - Historic New Bern Ride
description:
Team On Draft - Road Cycling
Bike MS is back in 2026! Put it on your calendar! While we don't know whether the weather will be perfect, soggy, or hot and muggy, we're gonna act like it'll be 80 degrees and sunny with a 90% chance of 202.2 miles of riding. And it's nearly two weeks later this year, so that improves our odds a bit.

The ride begins at Union Point Park, 210 E Front St, at 8 a.m. on Saturday, September 19. There will be routes of 30, 50, 75 and 100 miles on Saturday and again on Sunday.

We'll gather Friday evening at 6 p.m., either at our team tent in Union Point Park or at someone's Air BnB, for a team dinner and ride-strategy session.

Once you are prepared to throw yourselves into the awesomeness, you can join our team on our MS Society team page: [https://events.nationalmssociety.org/teams/99623](https://events.nationalmssociety.org/teams/99623) . Registration is now $50. The amount will go up a couple of times in the course of the summer; committing now will save you some money and also help the MS folks plan the ride.

Requirements:
Fundraising Minimum: $300
Age Minimum: 12
Awesomeness Minimum: 8.5/10.

If you have questions about logistics or fundraising, please contact Chris Bagley or post a comment below.

Please also use the comments section to organize groups for AirBnBs. The last couple of years, most of us have gotten together in groups to rent houses for the weekend. Camping in Union Point Park is free ... but also potentially wet.

title: Luminary & Freedom Stories
description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.

Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.

 

---

Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"

Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. Some took enormous risk to reach Union lines before the federal government made any promise of abolishing slavery. Others left their homes and plantations to follow Sherman's army as they marched through the southeast. Some believed home was where they already lived and worked and waited patiently for freedom to extend to them. Others still were lied to by their enslavers or moved away from the advancing U.S. Army so they would remain enslaved. Freedom came in different ways and at different times to enslaved people across the state.

One common thread unites these freedom stories: the defeat of the Confederate military ensured a new birth of freedom across the state and nation.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

title: John Hope Franklin Legacies Series | Caribbean Poetics: Nature and the Visual Arts
location: Smith Warehouse, Ahmadieh Family Lecture Hall, Bay 4, C105
description:
A central feature of Caribbean poetics has been a pictorial mode of representing the natural landscape and the complex multicultural societies that have taken root in the archipelago.  Verbal and visual arts converge in the creation of entangled ways of sensing and portraying the vulnerable yet resilient terrain of human interaction.
The Franklin Humanities Institute assembles an outstanding group of poets, artists, and scholars for a wide-ranging conversation about the interconnections between verbal depiction and visual aesthetics in the portrayal of the natural and socio-cultural worlds. 
The Caribbean offers a particularly fecund eco-site from which to engage in such a conversation. Sea and land, plantation and garden, hurricane and drought, cultivation and extraction, human and more-than-human life have long shaped the region's social histories and imaginative practices. Several generations of leading Caribbean poets have continually re-imagined the terms through which landscape, ecology, embodiment, memory, violence, beauty, and survival can be perceived, represented and understood.
Across a day and a half of presentations and conversations, the symposium addresses the question of how poetry in concert with the visual arts might help us to view these relations from an entangled perspective. How do poetic and visual practices intersect to register the histories deeply layered in Caribbean landscapes and seascapes? What might Caribbean poetics contribute to our thinking about the planetary ecological crisis, racialized histories, and possibilities for living otherwise?
Speakers:
Canisia Lubrin (University of Guelph)
Lizabeth Paravisini-Gebert (Vassar College)
Ishion Hutchinson (Cornell University)
Maria Cristina Fumagalli (University of Essex)
Mark McMorris (Georgetown University)
Kei Miller (University of Miami)
Manuel Arturo Abreu (Independent Researcher-Washington)

RSVP here

title: Lake James BioBlitz
location: Lake James State Park - Catawba River Access, Catawba River Access
description:
Join the North Carolina Native Plant Society Foothills Chapter and Lake James State Park for the Lake James BioBlitz on September 19, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.

A BioBlitz is a community science event focused on discovering and documenting as many species as possible in a designated area. Participants will explore Lake James State Park while searching for and identifying plants, animals, fungi, insects, and other organisms that make the park their home.

The event will begin with a talk from a Lake James State Park Ranger about local ecology before participants head into the field to explore diverse habitats and search for species. Whether you are an experienced naturalist or simply curious about the natural world, all skill levels are welcome. This is a great opportunity to learn more about the biodiversity of Lake James State Park while contributing valuable observations to our collective understanding of the park's natural resources.

Participants will use the iNaturalist app to document their discoveries. Before the event, attendees should download iNaturalist, create an account, and join the Lake James State Park BioBlitz Project. Observations submitted through the project will contribute to the event's community science data.

All skill levels are welcome. Minors must be accompanied by an adult. Refreshments will be provided.

Come explore, discover, and connect with the incredible biodiversity of Lake James State Park. Bring your curiosity and help us document the plants, animals, fungi, and other species that make this park unique.

Registration for the event is required.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

Join NCWF South Wake Conservationists Chapter at Inwood Wildlife Garden for a hands-on volunteer day as we build our first-ever hibernaculum! A hibernaculum is a protective shelter or refuge that wildlife uses to survive the winter dormancy period. Typically constructed using natural materials such as rocks, logs, branches, and stones, these structures create protected spaces for reptiles, amphibians, insects, and small mammals during the colder months. We’ll have the materials needed for construction on hand. 
Not into building a hibernaculum? We have plenty to do! There are lots of other ways to lend a hand at Inwood Wildlife Garden, including weeding the pollinator garden, mulching garden paths, planting aquatic plants around the wildlife pond, and helping with general garden maintenance. Feel free to BYOP: Bring Your Own Plant! Bring a native pollinator-friendly plant and add your own contribution to the Inwood Wildlife Garden. 
Whether you want to learn something new, get your hands dirty, or simply spend some time outside helping local wildlife, we’d love to have you join us!

Birders may get to catch a last glance of summertime birds like the summer tanager, black-and-white warbler, and great-crested flycatcher while hawks and falcons pass overhead! Leaves will begin showing signs of fall colors to come, with the green peaks and valleys of summer still visible before the cold season kicks off.

title: Screen/Society--"About Face: Disrupting Ballet" (2025) w/ dir. Jennifer Lin | AADS Symposium
description:
Special screening:

"About Face: Disrupting Ballet"
(Jennifer Lin, 2025, 60 min, USA, English, DCP)

ABOUT FACE: DISRUPTING BALLET is a feature-length documentary that spotlights Georgina Pazcoguin and Phil Chan, two friends and NYC dancers of Asian descent, who are challenging ballet companies to rid The Nutcracker and other ballets of offensive racial stereotypes. What started as a pledge on a website has grown into a global movement, disrupting the elite world of ballet.

Gina, a soloist with the New York City Ballet, and Phil, an author, producer and choreographer, launch the global "Final Bow for Yellowface" movement [https://www.yellowface.org]. They post an online pledge and ask dancers to jettison offensive "yellowface" caricatures from ballets like The Nutcracker and La Bayadère. Hundreds from around the world sign the pledge.

We watch in real time as the Scottish Ballet updates its version of the Chinese dance to both high praise and stinging backlash.

Phil takes on a bigger challenge of reimagining a full-length ballet: the problematic La Bayadére. Working with dancers at Indiana University, he boldly transports the story from ancient India to a Hollywood studio in the 1920s.

ABOUT FACE vividly shows the tension and risks the two artists endure as they push an art form-created for the entertainment of kings and queens hundreds of years ago-to more authentically reflect the American experience today.

"[O]ne thing unites myself, Jennifer Lin, and the dancers in the film: we are all of mixed-race Asian ancestry, navigating a duality that brings up persistent questions of identity and belonging. Lin's film offers catharsis, modeling attentive care that asks ballet to confront itself honestly, while also opening space for dialogue about representation. And for me, the film raises a difficult question: how do you love something that has also caused harm?" -- Lauren Berlin, thINKingDANCE 

==
About the filmmaker:

Jennifer Lin spent a lifetime as a reporter before turning to filmmaking a decade ago. During 32 years at The Philadelphia Inquirer, she served as a financial correspondent on Wall Street, a national correspondent in Washington, D.C., and an Asia correspondent in Beijing. Her first documentary, BEETHOVEN IN BEIJING, explored the Philadelphia Orchestra's legacy in China and subsequent films, TEN TIMES BETTER and ABOUT FACE: DISRUPTING BALLET, the examine the Asian American experience in ballet.

title: Duke Department of Music: Faculty & Student Gala Concert
description:
Celebrate the artistry, mentorship, and community at the heart of Duke Music during the 2026 Faculty & Student Gala Concert. This all-Mendelssohn program brings together distinguished faculty, accomplished alumni, and exceptional student musicians in honor of the retirement of renowned Mendelssohn scholar Dr. R. Larry Todd.

The program opens with the Duke Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Harry Davidson, performing the atmospheric Hebrides Overture, inspired by the dramatic Scottish landscape of Fingal's Cave. Next, pianist Bryan Tong joins the orchestra in a rare performance of Mendelssohn's unfinished Piano Concerto No. 3 in E Minor, meticulously reconstructed with the extraordinary musical scholarship and creativity of Dr. Todd.  

The evening culminates with the Ciompi Quartet of Duke University and alumni musicians of the Larkspur Quartet in a performance of Mendelssohn's exhilarating Octet for Strings; a youthful masterpiece brimming with irrepressible energy.

A reception honoring Dr. Todd will follow in the Mary Duke Biddle Music Building. Please RSVP using the link on this page.

Free and open to the public. All are welcome!

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Celebrating the Legacy of Alma Thomas and Black Artistry
location: Artspace, 201 East Davie Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
“Not Unlike Sunlight”: Celebrating the Legacy of Alma Thomas and Black Artistry Though Primary and Colorstruck!


Join acclaimed writers Alexis Pauline Gumbs and Richard J. Powell for a conversation celebrating the legacy of pioneering artist Alma Thomas and the enduring influence of Black artistry. 
Hosted on the closing day of All American: Contemporary Perspectives from HBCU Artists, the program brings Gumbs and Powell together in celebration of their new books, Primary and Colorstruck!. In Primary, Gumbs writes as a spiritual student of Thomas, offering a poetic response to Thomas’s life and work, while Colorstruck! draws upon Powell’s expansive scholarship on color, Black art, and visual culture, with Thomas among the artists considered throughout the book. 
As the first graduate of Howard University’s art department, Thomas holds an important place within the history of HBCU arts education and American abstraction. Through readings and conversation, Gumbs and Powell will reflect on her creative legacy, the possibilities of writing alongside visual art, and the many shades of Black artistic expression that continue to emerge in her wake. 
 
About the Authors 
Dr. Alexis Pauline Gumbs, author of Survival is a Promise: The Eternal Life of Audre Lorde is a queer Black feminist love evangelist and an aspirational cousin to all life. Publisher’s Weekly calls her writing “groundbreaking.” She is also the author of four earlier books aka portable textual ceremonies, including Undrowned which won the 2022 Whiting Award in Non-Fiction. A recipient of the Windham-Campbell Prize in Poetry, the National Endowment of the Arts Creative Writing Fellowship and a National Humanities Center Fellowship, Dr. Gumbs lives and loves in Durham, North Carolina. 
Dr. Richard J. Powell is the John Spencer Bassett Professor of Art & Art History at Duke University, where he has taught since 1989. Powell, an authority on African American art, has organized numerous art exhibitions, most notably: The Blues Aesthetic: Black Culture and Modernism (1989); Rhapsodies in Black: Art of the Harlem Renaissance (1997); To Conserve A Legacy: American Art at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (1999); Back to Black: Art, Cinema, and the Racial Imaginary (2005); and Archibald Motley: Jazz Age Modernist (2014). Powell has published books on numerous topics, including Homecoming: The Art and Life of William H. Johnson (1991), Black Art: A Cultural History (1997, 2002 & 2021), Cutting a Figure: Fashioning Black Portraiture (2008), Going There: Black Visual Satire (2020), and Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). From 2007 until 2010, Powell was Editor-in-Chief of The Art Bulletin, the world’s leading English language journal in art history. 
 
About Artspace 
Artspace is a non-profit visual arts center located in Downtown Raleigh. Visit Artspace to explore exhibitions featuring national and community artists, engage with more than 30 artists working in their studios, and enjoy art classes and community events for all ages and abilities. To learn more about Artspace, visit artspacenc.org 
 
Parking and Accessibility

title: Duke Arts Presents: Salix Piano Trio
description:
Experience the "probing, fiercely intelligent playing" (The Washington Post) of the Salix Piano Trio. Named for the "graceful and poetic weeping willow," the ensemble explores the chemistry between the violin, cello, and piano.  

Sample a range of musical wonders when the Salixes elicit 18th-century elegance in Mozart's Piano Trio No. 5 and the smoky, Romantic turbulence of Brahms's Piano Trio No. 1. Composer Frank Bridge adds a cafe sound to traditional dances, while Jennifer Higdon conjures lithe Impressionism in her trio movement "Pale Yellow." The centerpiece of the evening comes from the 16-year-old Dmitri Shostakovich, whose plucky trio runs between lyrical beauty and impudence.

The piano trio began as a house band, once gathered around the family harpsichord. Four hundred years on, this close-knit combination, now anchored by the piano, continues to captivate both players and audiences.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.

title: CEE Seminar - Biofilm Dispersion: Regulatory Mechanisms, Emergent Phenotypes, and Clinical Consequences
description: Biofilm dispersion is a regulated developmental transition that enables bacteria to exit surface‑attached communities and re‑enter a planktonic state. This seminar will examine the molecular circuitry that drives dispersion, with emphasis on the environmental cues, signaling pathways, and phosphodiesterase networks that coordinate matrix degradation and cell release. Emerging data reveal that dispersed cells represent a transcriptionally distinct physiological state. Their unique phenotype, including heightened susceptibility, increased motility, enhanced dissemination potential, immune evasion, and elevated virulence traits, will be discussed. These features have important clinical implications, positioning dispersed cells as key contributors to biofilm persistence, dissemination, and the establishment of secondary infections, while also highlighting dispersion as a therapeutically relevant intervention point for biofilm control.

description:

The Campus, located between Boone and Blowing Rock, has become a community hub with a rain garden for stormwater runoff, native landscape around the office, half acre pollinator garden trail, 2.2-mile public hiking trail, shrub transition zone for wildlife habitat between the forest and field, and an agricultural plot growing food for the community. 
During this workday, we will direct our effort toward planting native plants and building deer proof cages to contribute to the larger ongoing stream and wetland restoration project on campus. This project will transform a former cattle grazing pasture into healthy aquatic and terrestrial habitat with riparian and vernal pool plantings along 800 linear feet of Aho Branch. Numerous wildlife species will benefit from this project including yellow-spotted salamanders and brook trout.

title: CDVS Workshop: Meeting Data Management and Sharing Plan Requirements
description: There are many federal and private funders who require data management (and sharing) plans as part of a grant application. NIH implemented a new Data Management and Sharing Policy in early 2023 and other funding agencies, such as NSF, are implementing revised public access and data sharing policies in early 2025 to comply with the "Nelson Memo" and the Gold Standard of Science. This workshop will cover the components of a data management and sharing plan, what makes a strong plan and how to adhere to it, and where to find guidance, tools, resources, and assistance for building funder-based plans. We will also discuss how to make data management plans actionable and meaningful living documents to support research integrity, reproducibility, reuse, and verification of results. This workshop is a collaboration of Duke University Libraries, the Office of Scientific Integrity, and the Medical Center Libraries and Archives. This event is open to non-Duke participants. This workshop is eligible for 2 hours of Graduate School RCR Credit (GS714) and 200-level faculty and staff RCR.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Prove What Your Agent Did
description:
All Things AI (Live)
Most agent governance answers stop at "here are our logs". A counterparty who does not work for you has no particular reason to accept that, and those are the people asking. The TRACE Registry is a public append-only record of agent evidence, with signed checkpoints, an offline verifier, and a page stating what it does and does not prove. Action State runs a free public witness: any log can send it a checkpoint, a few hundred bytes carrying no payload, and get back a receipt anyone can verify without calling either company. On September 7 the registry sent a checkpoint to a witness operated by a company it does not own, and the receipt verified from published bytes using a public key and open source code, with no network calls. We will run that verification live, including the two fields the receipt deliberately leaves false, and Mark will take questions.

description: Every day, the blood in our bodies performs an extraordinary balancing act: flowing freely through our vessels when we are healthy, yet rapidly forming clots when we are injured to prevent dangerous blood loss. Join this installation of Research Cafe to hear Dr. Yuriy Prokopenko, MD, an expert in hemophilia, tell us about this remarkable process and how hemophilia affects it. title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

Readers are:
• Crystina
• Naveed
• Kendall

Backup Readers are:
• Allegra
• Baxter
• Sigma

Deep Backup:
• Anna

***

***We meet every Tuesday at the same time, but alternate between In-Person*** ***and on Zoom. Members may attend both formats, if desired, but readers will be listed separately under the In-Person or Zoom weeks.***

title: Travel CHINA like a local! Virtual QnA [x-posted]
description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group
Putting out feelers for curious, cooperative 'comrades' to explore quiet corners of Old Cathay! Trip date TBD - waiting for airfares to come down.

This will happen on Google Meet.

**CHECK THE COMMENTS FOR MEETING LINK!**

[Comment if you are able to log onto the link but don't see me - in the past Google has let two meetings with the same link open, each person thinking the other didn't show up. So comment here and we'll see if we can fix it. :-) ]

I've been traveling to China for 27 years. Join me for a unique, off the beaten track culture immersion adventure!

Comfort NOT guaranteed! LOTS of walking! This trip is NOT for everyone but everyone who has come with me so far has LOVED it!

Itinerary NOT guaranteed so as to maximize experience! Spontaneous private zheng concert in a riverside pavilion? Let's stop and enjoy! Weather is forecast to be rain in the mountains? Let's go to the ancient village instead.

Costs currently unknown but should be under $100/day for ALL in-country necessities: food, lodging, entrance fees, ground transport. Whatever price I end up quoting will NOT include transport to/from China, alcohol, upgrades to lodging\*, upgrades to in-country transport\*.

You can do it cheaper with a big box tour. If strict time schedules, overpriced shopping, industrial restaurant food, and being kept away from locals is good enough for you than that's your best bet. If unique, real China, great food, insider knowledge with eye for western comforts\*\*, and turn on a dime\*\*\* [a mao?] escapades are for you than come with me!

Only seven people! Small and 'nimble'\*\*\*!

Have you already been to China? Already have seen the Forbidden City and Great Wall? No worries! Big box tours do NOT go where I go!

Have you never been to China and NEED to see the big sights? No problem! I can create an optional 3 day add-on for the Great Wall, Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, and other Beijing highlights. AND I can take you to hidden gems few big tours touch.

Let's dialog! Looking for like minded people so everyone's on the same page. Don't want to put hard-core shoppers with shop-hating history buffs, or long distance hikers with casual strollers. Just a more practical way to go. If enough interest I can lead TWO trips, each with its own emphasis. I reserve the right to group/accept/deny as I see fit. [I only want happiness! Sometimes that means saying 'maybe next time'.]

Go to Jan Tu Tours on FB and browse the photo albums to get a hint of what one might see. No guarantees of ANYTHING! China changes very quickly.

\*Where available - LOTS of things NOT available off the beaten track. I said 'adventure'!

\*\*Sometimes western comforts are just not there. Deep in the countryside villages rarely have western toilets.

\*\*\*Quick change of plans is relative in China; western expectations are best set aside and an embrace the new/unknown/surprise attitude is highly recommended. But that's what a cultural adventure is all about!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.
source: NC State African American Cultural Center

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

Understand the preattentive process and how it affects visual perceptionCritically evaluate the accuracy and quality of visualizations they encounter in their daily livesImplement best practices when creating their own visualizations

title: The 1776 North Carolina Constitution
description:
North Carolina’s 1776 Constitution grew out of two crises: an east-west power struggle that erupted into the War of the Regulation, and a fight for political representation against an increasingly hostile English government. This lecture traces that story back to the religious and political conflicts of 17th-century Britain, through the migrations and economic pressures that shaped colonial North Carolina, to the document that remains the state’s constitutional foundation today. 

 

The lecture is presented by an interdisciplinary team from Carolina Law, the History Department and the University Libraries.

title: Lectures in Art History: Art, Health, Equity Series featuring Amanda Cachia, Arizona State University
description:
“Access, Activism, and Aesthetic Revision: Crip Methods for Art History”

 

This talk brings together the core arguments of The Agency of Access: Contemporary Disability Art and Institutional Critique (2024), Hospital Aesthetics: Disability, Medicine, Activism (2025), and Rehabilitating the Asylum: Mental Health Justice and Contemporary Art (2027) to demonstrate that disability is not peripheral to canonical art; instead, it is one of its most generative methodological engines to arise with the canon of 20th century art history. Across these three books, Amanda Cachia develops what she calls a critical-aesthetic approach to access, care, and confinement, tracing how hospitals, asylums, and contemporary art institutions function as overlapping architectures of power, creativity, and resistance. Moving between art history, disability studies, medical humanities, institutional critique, and the activist strategies of contemporary disability artists, Cachia shows how access operates as an artistic medium and how care becomes an aesthetic category. By centering disability as both method and material, she proposes an art history that is structurally transformed by the politics and poetics of access, and how pertinent historical artworks and movements can be reconfigured based on a crip revision. 

 

Amanda Cachia is Professor of Practice in Museum Studies in the School of Art at the Herberger Institute for Design and the Arts at Arizona State University and Affiliate Faculty in the Disability Studies B.A. Her research interests include disability art history, theory and activism, crip curatorial practices and access aesthetics, museums, institutional critique, and social justice, and critical disability approaches to translation, movement, medicine, and health. Cachia is the author of three books, Rehabilitating the Asylum: Mental Health Justice and Contemporary Art, (forthcoming 2027), Hospital Aesthetics: Disability, Medicine, Activism (2025), and The Agency of Access: Contemporary Disability Art and Institutional Critique (2024), the latter of which was shortlisted for the College Art Association’s 2026 Charles Rufus Morey Book Award. She is also editor of Curating Access: Disability Art Activism and Creative Accommodation (2022), which includes over 40 international contributors. She is currently working on her fourth book project, Disability Art: A Political History. Since 2010, Cachia has organized 20 art exhibitions devoted to the work of disabled artists. She is currently developing the major touring exhibition Vital Signs: From Patient to Power with Mid-America Arts Alliance and ExhibitsUSA, which will be hosted by numerous galleries across the United States from 2027-2032. Cachia is also a curatorial and disability advisor for a major exhibition being developed about art and disability from the 19th century to the present at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in 2028.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Generative AI and Survey Research: Foundations, Applications, and the Respondent Experience
description:
This course explores the potential applications of generative AI (gen AI) for survey research. Designed for survey practitioners, data scientists, and social scientists, it provides an introduction to Gen AI – especially large language models (LLMs) – and delves into their applications across the survey lifecycle. Participants will gain foundational knowledge of how AI technologies like LLMs work, understand its implications for survey data quality (in relation to frameworks such as Total Survey Error), and learn practical strategies for integrating GenAI into survey design, data collection, and analysis. Rather than focusing on the technical aspects of LLMs, this course will focus on applied AI research, drawing on empirical evidence of how LLMs perform in areas such as conversational interviewing and synthetic response generation. We will pay particular attention to model evaluation, responsible management of risks, user experience design (UXD), and the augmentation (not replacement) of human expertise.

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access.

This events is sponsored by the UNC Odum Institue for Research in Social Science.

title: Sept 24 - AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup on September 24 to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Date, Time and Location**

Sep 24, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-september-24-2026)**

**How Do Mercedes-Benz AI Principles Drive our Innovation?**

At Mercedes-Benz, our AI Principles guide every step of innovation, emphasizing responsible use, safety and reliability, explainability, and the protection of privacy. These principles go beyond statements and actively shape how we design, test, and deploy AI systems in real-world automotive and enterprise settings. In this talk, I will present how these principles inspired our recent research on when reusing LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is effective. By combining theoretical analysis with synthetic data as a proxy for enterprise scenarios, we uncovered the strengths and limitations of modular AI components under constrained data access. Our findings provide practical guidance on when reused LoRAs could deliver high-quality results.

*About the Speaker*

[Mei-Yen Chen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mei-yen-chen-22937787) is a Senior Data Scientist at Mercedes-Benz Tech Innovation GmbH in Germany with 10 years of industry experience in AI and data solutions. She leads early-stage AI projects across business functions and collaborates with research institutions on machine learning and responsible AI.

**Region Tokens as the Visual Primitive: From Recognition to World Modeling**

Patch-based tokenization has become the default interface between vision encoders and downstream models, yet patches carry no semantic structure and scale poorly with resolution and temporal extent. This talk presents a research program centered on replacing patch tokens with region-level representations — semantically dense tokens grounded in visual entities rather than arbitrary grid crops.

I will describe RELOCATE, REN, and T-REN, a progression of methods that produce region tokens via pooling, train them with region-level objectives, and extend them to video with temporal coherence. I will then present ongoing work integrating region tokens into VLMs to directly expand visual context capacity, and preliminary results on future region trajectory prediction as a foundation for world modeling.

The broader thesis is that region-level tokens are a more natural unit of visual computation than patches, and their advantage compounds as task complexity, resolution, and temporal horizon increase.

*About the Speaker*

[Savya Khosla](https://www.linkedin.com/in/savyakhosla/) is a second-year Ph.D. student at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, advised by Prof. Derek Hoiem and Prof. Alex Schwing.

**Leveraging Text-To-Image Diffusion Models for Consistent Set-to-Set Generation**

Image collections are humans' primary way of capturing the world, yet advances in generative editing remain largely inapplicable to this modality. We address this gap by introducing Match-and-Fuse - a zero-shot, training-free method for consistent set-to-set generation from image collections that share a common visual element but differ in viewpoint, capture time, and surrounding content.
Our key idea is a unified graph-based framework that combines dense correspondences with an emergent prior in text-to-image diffusion models to generate coherent canvases. We achieve state-of-the-art consistency and visual quality, and unlock new creative capabilities for content generation.

*About the Speaker*

[Kate Feingold](https://www.linkedin.com/in/katefeingold/) is a PhD student in Computer Vision at the Weizmann Institute of Science. Her research sits at the intersection of generative models, 3D/4D perception, and multimodal learning, focusing on problems where vision meets other modalities or paradigms in creative tasks.

**Yield Estimation of a Coffee in a dense environment**

This presentation provides a detailed workflow related to coffee yield estimation in a dense environment. With photos of pre-harvest coffee plants from a couple of coffee estates, details related to pre-processing, annotation to detect regions of interest (ROI), object detection training and inferencing results with various Yolo models and finally segmentation with SAM2 and Yolo\*-seg with training and inference results to determine the count of raw, pre-mature, mature and over-mature coffee berries and finally the yield of the entire estate. All this is based on real world data captured on iPhone and android phones.

*About the Speaker*

[Raghu M. Rao](http://www.linkedin.com/in/raghumrao) is a consultant working on applications of computer vision AI models. He was previously with AMD and Xilinx. He has a Ph.D. in Wireless Communications from UCLA and is a Senior Member, IEEE. His current interests are in applications of AI for agriculture, health care and wireless communications.
