title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Mining Society Merit Badge Workshop
description:
Registered Scouts will have the opportunity to complete all requirements needed to earn the “Mining in Society” merit badge at Reed Gold Mine’s merit badge workshop.

The workshop begins with a PowerPoint presentation and class time to finish the sections of the “Mining in Society” merit badge workbook. After completing the in-class portion, Scouts will be taken on a guided tour of the underground mine and learn about Reed Gold Mine’s history and learn more about the gold mining process. Following that, weather permitting, Scouts will be able to pan for gold in the outdoor panning area.

There is a $15 registration fee per Scout, which includes the cost of the workshop, tour, and one panning ticket (weather permitting). Adult leaders and chaperones who wish to pan with their Scouts can purchase a panning ticket in the gift shop. Panning tickets are sold on a first come, first served basis and are $4.00 after tax. Adult leaders and chaperones may also buy a tour ticket if they’re interested in going on the guided tour of the underground mine. Tour tickets are $5.00 for adults 13 and older.

In 2026, “Mining in Society” merit badge workshops will be offered May 9, June 13, July 11, August 8, September 12, October 10, and November 14. Each workshop begins at 10:00 am and runs until 2:00 pm and is limited to 60 participants.

Registration form- https://tinyurl.com/5ubvkkkc

For more information and to schedule, contact Reed Gold Mine’s Education Coordinator, Logan Stamper. He can be reached by email at logan.stamper@dncr.nc.gov or by phone at (704) 721-4653.

Al Strong Quintet

The Al Strong Quintet is a powerhouse ensemble rooted in the vibrant jazz tradition, infused with the energy and innovation of contemporary sounds. Led by the multi-talented trumpeter, composer, and teaching artist Al Strong, the group is celebrated for its soulful performances, dynamic arrangements, and genre-blurring creativity.

A native of Washington, D.C., Strong has long set his roots in the Raleigh-Durham area and earned a reputation as a leading voice in modern jazz. With a sound that bridges classic swing, Afro-Cuban rhythms, and modern grooves, his artistic vision has captivated audiences worldwide. Al is a 2x Grammy Nominated contributor/producer and has had the pleasure of performing with some of modern music’s most notable figures; Aretha Franklin, Sullivan Fortner, Sigur Ros, Rissi Palmer, Kirk Whalum, Branford Marsalis, The Foreign Exchange, and Old Crow Medicine Show.

Sidecar Social Club

Spirited, stylish, and engaging, Sidecar Social Club is a shot of whiskey hitting your veins. Effortlessly crossing genres, their energetic performances transport audiences to surprising places—from the gritty underbelly of speakeasy jazz and wartime cabarets to Latin dance halls, the big band era, soulful R&B, and '50s rock. With infectious originals mixed into their sets, SSC delivers a fresh, artful take on both classic and contemporary music.

Known for their dynamic stage presence, SSC has performed at venues and events such as Artsplosure, The NC Governor's Ball, The South Carolina Jazz Festival, The Apex Jazz Festival, The North Carolina Museum of Art, and The Bechtler Museum of Modern Art, as well as iconic spots like The Umstead Hotel, Kings Barcade, and MOTORCO. Whether creating an elegant atmosphere or igniting a lively celebration, Sidecar Social Club brings seasoned style and panache to every event, leaving audiences enthralled and entertained.

Bittersweet Brass Band

The Bittersweet Brass Band is the latest high-energy project from two-time Grammy-nominated trumpeter Al Strong. As the second brass band founded by Strong, this ensemble not only delivers an electrifying, modern take on the New Orleans brass band tradition, but also serves as a vital training ground for young, aspiring musicians—offering them real-world, professional performance experience while sharing the joy and cultural richness of New Orleans music. Blending the soulful roots of traditional brass band sounds with contemporary influences, Bittersweet Brass creates one of the most dynamic and engaging dance band experiences around

title: NC the Beautiful: Invasive Plant Purge
location: Haw River State Park - Iron Ore Belt Access
description:
“Invasive” plants are introduced, aggressively-growing plants that negatively impact local ecosystems. Join park staff at Haw River State Park’s Iron Ore Belt Access to help remove these leafy invaders! 

Typical workdays start with paperwork for new volunteers (less than five minutes) followed by a short hike to the work area where volunteers will receive instruction on how to identify the target species of the day. The rest of the time will be used on employing hands-on, seasonally appropriate techniques to remove invasive plants from the landscape, helping to restore the area for native plants and wildlife. 

Advance registration is required as supplies and space are limited. This opportunity is only open to volunteers ages 12 and up. Any volunteers under the age of 16 must be registered with and accompanied by an adult. 

Volunteers should wear long sleeves, long pants, and close-toed shoes. Please bring work gloves and loppers or pruning shears if you have them, but if not they will be provided (and you don't need to let us know in advance either way). Meet at the parking lot of the Iron Ore Belt Access.

title: TALsounds | CMM 26-27
description:
FEATURING

TALsounds

Natalie Chami (TALsounds) is a Canadian-born Lebanese American musician and educator based in Alexandria, VA. Known for her work in drone, ambient, and improvisational music, she blends vintage analog synthesizers, operatic vocals, and immersive atmospheres into distinctive sound worlds. Chami has released music on Ba Da Bing, NNA Tapes, and Hausu Mountain, toured across the U.S., Canada, and Europe, and received coverage from Pitchfork, The Fader, The Washington Post, and The Chicago Tribune. Her latest album, Shift (2023), departs from her warm analog palette and explores FM and digital synthesis, featuring contributions from SWANA women in production, art, and photography. 

Chami was founding Vocal Chair at The Chicago High School for the Arts (2009–2021), developing the voice department and trauma-informed, anti-racist curriculum. She also leads workshops at universities, scores films, creates sound installations, and is the Category Content Specialist for Synthesizers at KORG USA. In 2025, she was invited to serve on Experimental Sound Studio’s first-ever Artist Advisory Council, supporting the development of new online programming for artists in electronic and sound art.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission
description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.

The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.

Commission meetings are held quarterly to review applications and discuss Certification policies and procedures.

The commission's meeting dates for the 2025-2026 year are October 27, 2025, January 9, 2026, April 10, 2026, and July 10, 2026. All meetings are held at the Library of NC beginning at 1:00 pm unless otherwise posted. Information about meetings can be found on the North Carolina Secretary of State's meeting calendar.

Have questions about certification? Contact us at NC.Certification.Commission@dncr.nc.gov.

Spooky season is here, and we’re brewing up something a little different. 👻

Join Triangle Third Place and Discover Durham Together at Drink a Bull in Durham for an LGBTQ+ mixer filled with tea, cocktails, mocktails, new connections, and just enough Halloween chaos.

Come meet people. Collect some bracelets. Spill a little tea. Maybe cast a spell or two.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: Renée Fleming in Recital Voice of Nature: the Anthropocene
description:
When was the last time a performance changed the way you looked at the world around you? 

Voice of Nature: the Anthropocene is an exploration of one of the defining issues of our time—environmental change—through music and imagery. It invites us to consider the beauty and fragility of the natural world and our relationship to it.

Performed by acclaimed soprano Renée Fleming, the program pairs classical songs and contemporary works with an original film created in partnership with the National Geographic Society. The experience is both intimate and expansive, sharing landscapes of breathtaking beauty alongside acute reminders of their vulnerability.

 

At a moment when environmental change increasingly shapes everyday life, Voice of Nature reminds us that these challenges are not just scientific or political; they are deeply personal. It is an invitation to consider how rapidly the natural world is changing while reflecting on how much we rely on its constancy for solace, inspiration, and a sense of connection to something larger than ourselves.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets  at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/voice-of-nature/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Engagement in Research 101
description:
Engagement in Research 101: Introduction to Engaging Patient & Community Partners in Research

 

Are you interested in learning about patient and community engagement and how it can benefit your research? Excited by the idea of engaging patient, community, or other partners in your research, but unsure about where to start? Want to know more about how to engage partners at different points throughout your study?

 

Engaging with patient and community partners who are impacted by your research can be instrumental to the success of your study. This online training will provide an overview of engagement in research, highlighting that engagement is not "all or nothing" or "one-size-fits-all", but instead encompasses a wide variety of low touch to high touch approaches that could be right for your study.

 

The session will cover common myths/misconceptions about engagement in research, benefits of and key considerations for engaging patient and community partners in research, and initial steps/existing resources you can leverage to begin engaging partners in your research.

 

Register

 

Presenters:
Alicia Bilheimer, MPH - Director of Engaged Science, NC TraCS
Veronica Carlisle, MPH, CHES - Senior Community Health Educator, UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center (LCCC)
Nisha Datta, MS - Senior Project Manager, NC TraCS
Simone Frank, MPH - Senior Project Manager, NC TraCS
Jennifer Potter, MPH, CHES - Senior Program Coordinator for Clinical Outreach, LCCC

 

Engaging Patient, Community, and Other Partners in Your Research is a multi-part online training series. You may register for the entire series OR any single training session. This training series was developed collaboratively with patient, community, and researcher partners and is co-sponsored by the UNC Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center and NC TraCS Institute.

title: Botany Spotlight: Meet the Meat Eaters—Carnivorous Plants
location: Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Enter the remarkable world of carnivorous plants with Alec Motten, professor emeritus, Duke University Department of Biology. Start in the classroom with an overview of the impressive array of structures that make carnivory possible—from digestive glands and sticky traps to slippery pitfalls, trap doors and snap-shut jaws. Look closely at these structures under a microscope, then venture outside to meet specimens living in the garden. Whether you’re captivated by the iconic Venus flytrap’s sudden snap, the drowning pools and pit-fall traps of pitcher plants or the elegant patience of a sundew’s glistening tentacles, this program will forever change the way you think about what plants are capable of. Pair this class with a tour of the Duke Research Greenhouse’s teaching collection, which includes an impressive collection of carnivorous plants, on Saturday, November 21 (register separately). 
Location: Pelham-Cullen Classroom inside the Barnes Welcome Center. 
Fee: $28, 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Parking fees apply.

The indoor location is equipped with a hearing loop, which transmits sound directly to hearing aids and cochlear implants with a T-coil setting. Accessible restrooms are available onsite.

title: Renée Fleming Music & Mind
description:
What happens in your brain when music moves you to tears? What can we advance in neuroscience when a researcher asks why a melody can unlock a memory, ease anxiety, or help a patient heal? 

 

For years, Renée Fleming has worked alongside physicians and researchers to better understand the profound relationship between music and human health. In this conversation, presented in partnership with the UNC School of Medicine and moderated by arts and culture journalist Liza Roberts, Fleming and UNC neuroscientists and practitioners explore how the arts are informing cutting-edge developments and reshaping clinical practice.

 

The discussion moves beyond theory and into applications that touch everyday life: how creative experiences matter to your well-being, and how scientists are establishing important roles for the arts in healing, connection, and human flourishing.

 

This is a rare opportunity to hear artists, scientists, and medical professionals share the same stage and to discover how one of humanity’s oldest forms of expression is shaping the future of health care.

 

Please note: Renée Fleming will not be performing during this program. Join us for her separately-ticketed performance on October 13.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/musicmind/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Oct 15 - AI, ML, and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Time, Place and Location**

Oct 15, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-october-15-2026)**

**Testing AI Systems in Production: Data Quality, Drift, and Model Evaluation**

AI systems can pass offline evaluation and still fail in production when real-world data changes, features become stale, labels or feedback signals are incomplete, or model behavior drifts away from expected outcomes. This talk shares practical patterns for testing and evaluating AI systems after deployment, including data quality checks, drift detection, online/offline metric comparison, model monitoring, and rollback analysis.

Using personalization and recommendation systems as examples, we will examine how teams can build evaluation workflows that catch quality issues before users do. Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for making AI-backed systems easier to evaluate, debug, and operate as data changes over time.

*About the Speaker*

[Jayakumar Ramalingam](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jayakumarramalingam) is a Staff Software Engineer and Cloud Architect at SiriusXM with over 16 years of experience building cloud-native platforms, real-time data pipelines, resilient APIs, and AI/ML-enabled applications at production scale.

**Where Should Your Model Live? A Framework for Tiering Computer Vision Deployments**

Where should a computer vision model actually run - on-device, near the edge, or in the cloud? It's a decision that looks simple until requirements like latency, cost, connectivity, and update cadence start pulling in different directions, often revealing themselves only after deployment.

Drawing on hands-on experience developing and deploying CV models across Hailo, Nvidia, Qualcomm and AWS platforms, this talk introduces a practical framework for tiering computer vision deployments based on real project requirements and constraints. Discussion will include what changes at each tier - from development to deployment to monitoring and update strategy - with relevant industry examples.

Attendees will leave with a set of questions or a framework they can use to place their own CV projects into the right tier.

*About the Speaker*

[Ajaykumaar Sivacoumare](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ajay-sa/) is an AI Software Engineer specializing in computer vision and edge AI, with production experience developing and deploying CV models across Nvidia, Hailo, Qualcomm and AWS-based platforms.

**From 2D Slices to 3D Tumors: Lightweight Volumetric Detection Without Heavy 3D Networks**

Slice-wise 2D detectors are fast and scalable, but they struggle to produce reliable 3D bounding boxes from volumetric medical data. This talk presents YOLO-PVC, a lightweight post-processing framework that consolidates slice-wise YOLO detections into coherent 3D bounding boxes using percentile-based geometric aggregation and a minimal MLP calibration module.

This talk demonstrates consistent improvements in volumetric IoU across three liver tumor categories i.e., HCC, CCA, and Mixed, without requiring dense 3D annotations or memory-intensive architectures. The talk covers the clinical motivation, the technical approach, and practical lessons from deploying computer vision on real hospital MRI data.

*About the Speaker*

[Talha Waqas](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mtalha-waqas-255557144/) is a second-year PhD student at ESME Research Lab, Paris and LISSI, Université Paris-Est, working on computer vision applied to medical imaging, with a focus on tumor classification, detection, and segmentation in multi-phase liver MRI.

**The Two-Loop Architecture for Voice AI**

Building responsive voice AI requires balancing latency with intelligence. This talk introduces a practical architecture that separates real-time conversation from asynchronous reasoning, enabling richer interactions without slowing the user experience. The session covers reusable design patterns drawn from production-inspired conversational AI systems.

*About the Speaker*

[Abhinav Tushar](https://lepisma.xyz/wiki/about/) is an ML engineer and researcher specializing in Conversational AI and Speech Technology.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: The Single Source of Truth: Building Data Foundations for Agentic AI
description:
Data Science Raleigh
Traditional data management was built to give humans consistent, trustworthy records to work from. Agentic AI demands something more dynamic: data that agents can query, reason over, and act on continuously, without waiting for a human to interpret it first. That shift changes what "good" data actually looks like.

This webinar explores how data foundations must evolve to support agentic AI—moving from static, periodically-updated records toward connected, real-time, machine-consumable data. We'll cover what it takes to make data not just accurate, but usable by autonomous systems making decisions at machine speed.

**Key Takeaways:**

1️⃣ **Rethinking "Good" Data:** How agentic AI changes the requirements for data quality and structure.

2️⃣ **Real-Time Unification:** Why static, periodic data processes fall short for continuously acting agents.

3️⃣ **Machine-Readable Trust:** Designing authoritative records that agents can reliably reason over.

4️⃣ **Data Stewardship for Autonomy:** How data ownership roles must adapt as agents become primary data consumers.

**[Register here](https://datasciconnect.com/events/webinars/single-source-of-truth/)**

title: CSA Triangle October Meet-Up | Governing Agentic Work
description:
Cloud Security Alliance Triangle Chapter
**Governing Agentic Work: An Open Architecture for AI Workforce Adoption**

**Summary of Presentation:**
Moving beyond AI chatbots means trusting agents to build applications, reach internal systems, and run repeatable workflows. That trust cannot be granted with a long-lived API key. In this session, Johnnie Tabron draws on Cloudflare's own internal experience and the newly open-sourced Cloudflare OS architecture to show what it actually takes to put agents to work safely.

Attendees will see how organizational context and reusable skills keep agents aligned to established terminology, procedures, and standards, and how a conversation becomes an editable document, a connected application, and a mostly deterministic workflow. They will also learn why capability-based access beats handing credentials to agents and generated code. From there, the talk walks through the governance layer that constrains agent authority, controls where observed data moves, and preserves human accountability, before showing how every step gets centralized oversight and how agents finally ship as isolated, full-stack applications that any organization can deploy and customize in its own Cloudflare account.

Benefits-led but security-focused, the session's central message is that useful enterprise AI demands more than controlling the first model or tool call. Designed for security leaders, architects, cloud and platform engineers, developers, GRC professionals, and AI practitioners, the talk is presented through diagrams, architecture visuals, and interface examples, followed by Q&A.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Pruning with Confidence: Small Trees and Shrubs
location: Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Whether you’ve been nervously eyeing an overgrown branch or just want to keep your trees healthy and beautiful for years to come, this practical pruning workshop with Bobby Mottern, director of horticulture at Duke Gardens, gives you the knowledge and confidence to pick up your pruners. 
You’ll start indoors with a slide presentation on pruning principles, you’ll learn: 

Why trees need pruning — and what happens when they don’t get it
When is the best time to prune for tree health
What to remove — and just as importantly, what to leave alone
How to make clean, proper cuts that help trees heal
Which tools to use, how to maintain them and how to stay safe on the job

Then head outside into the garden, where you’ll see techniques demonstrated and get the chance to try them yourself. You’ll leave with practical skills and the confidence to approach pruning in your garden. 
Fee: $28; 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Location: Pelham-Cullen Classroom inside the Barnes Welcome Center. 
Accessibility: This will be a small group program that takes place partially seated indoors and partially outdoors, traveling on a combination of paved and unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and moderate inclines. The indoor location is equipped with a hearing loop, which transmits sound directly to hearing aids and cochlear implants with a T-coil setting. Accessible restrooms are available onsite.

title: John Lawson Legacy Days
description:
Step back in time and experience the history of eastern North Carolina during the 15th Annual John Lawson Legacy Days, hosted by the Grifton Historical Museum & Indian Village.

This multi-day living history event brings the past to life through historical demonstrations, reenactors, guest speakers, exhibits, hands-on activities, period crafts, and educational programs exploring the people and events that shaped North Carolina. Visitors can learn about explorer and naturalist John Lawson, Native American history and culture, colonial life, early settlement, and the rich heritage of eastern North Carolina.

The 2026 celebration will be especially meaningful as John Lawson Legacy Days coincides with the 50th anniversary of the Grifton Historical Museum and the nationwide America250 commemoration of the 250th anniversary of American independence.

Programs throughout the weekend will offer something for history lovers of all ages, from living history and demonstrations to special presentations and family-friendly activities. The weekend will also include opportunities to explore the museum and discover the fascinating history found right here in eastern North Carolina.

Join us October 16–18, 2026, as we celebrate 15 years of John Lawson Legacy Days, 50 years of preserving Grifton's history, and 250 years of America's story.

Location: Grifton Historical Museum & Indian Village, Grifton, NC

title: Park Hangs: Real Companion
description:
Unwind and socialize at Park Hangs, an outdoor concert series at Bailey Park

Gather and unwind to the alt-country rock sounds of Real Companion from 6:00–8:00 pm. Food truck service begins at 5:00 pm.

Based in Boone, Real Companion is an alt-country rock and folk-adjacent outfit fronted by Seth Sullivan. Their debut full-length album Nü-metal Heroes was recorded in a backyard studio, drawing inspiration from a winding path towards sobriety, parenthood, and cheeseburgers.

“Nü-metal Heroes feels off-the-cuff but fully developed—whether the duo are trying their hand at spirited country-rockers or more streamlined, almost dreamy folk-pop, their instrumental contributions are pleasing but never taking away from the yarns Sullivan spins at the center of the songs. It all amounts to a palpably Appalachian rock record—one that isn’t constrained by its roots, but that bears the marks of them nonetheless.”
— Rosy Overdrive

 

Park Hangs

Join us to unwind and socialize at a new outdoor concert series with music by NC-based artists, food and drinks by local vendors, and easygoing vibes in Bailey Park (445 Patterson Ave. in Winston-Salem). title: Spill the Tea!
location: Arts of the Albemarle, Maguire Theatre
description:
​Spill the Tea! is a bold new musical inspired by the first recorded act of women's activism in American history — the Edenton Tea Party. At the heart of the story is Penelope Barker, the daring woman who organized 50 other women to sign a public resolution boycotting British goods — and sent it directly to King George III. This radical act of defiance, carried out in a time when women had no political voice, helped spark a revolution and laid the groundwork, not only for the birth of a new nation, but for women to stand up for their rights.

Blending pop, hip-hop, orchestral, and classic Broadway musical styles, Spill the Tea! is filled with humor, heart, and history. With a witty script plus lavish sets and costumes, the show celebrates the power of those who refused to stay silent.​

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Play the Cyber Bowl
description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy. 

 

All October long, students, faculty and staff can log into the Cyber Bowl website and take a short cybersecurity quiz. Each completed quiz earns a point for Carolina.

 

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. In the inaugural Cyber Bowl, Carolina won the championship by garnering the largest participation by percentage. Last year, Carolina fielded the most players — almost 2,000 — of any school.

 

The Cyber Bowl is sponsored by Information Technology Services and the Information Security Office as part of National Cybersecurity Awareness Month.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Spill the Tea!
location: Arts of the Albemarle, Maguire Theatre
description:
​Spill the Tea! is a bold new musical inspired by the first recorded act of women's activism in American history — the Edenton Tea Party. At the heart of the story is Penelope Barker, the daring woman who organized 50 other women to sign a public resolution boycotting British goods — and sent it directly to King George III. This radical act of defiance, carried out in a time when women had no political voice, helped spark a revolution and laid the groundwork, not only for the birth of a new nation, but for women to stand up for their rights.

Blending pop, hip-hop, orchestral, and classic Broadway musical styles, Spill the Tea! is filled with humor, heart, and history. With a witty script plus lavish sets and costumes, the show celebrates the power of those who refused to stay silent.​

title: Play the Cyber Bowl
description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy.

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. In the inaugural Cyber Bowl, Carolina won the championship by garnering the largest participation by percentage. Last year, Carolina fielded the most players — almost 2,000 — of any school.

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Spill the Tea!
location: Arts of the Albemarle, Maguire Theatre
description:
​Spill the Tea! is a bold new musical inspired by the first recorded act of women's activism in American history — the Edenton Tea Party. At the heart of the story is Penelope Barker, the daring woman who organized 50 other women to sign a public resolution boycotting British goods — and sent it directly to King George III. This radical act of defiance, carried out in a time when women had no political voice, helped spark a revolution and laid the groundwork, not only for the birth of a new nation, but for women to stand up for their rights.

Blending pop, hip-hop, orchestral, and classic Broadway musical styles, Spill the Tea! is filled with humor, heart, and history. With a witty script plus lavish sets and costumes, the show celebrates the power of those who refused to stay silent.​

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Mapping What Matters: A Workshop on Logic Models for Program Evaluation
description:
The Odum Institute in collaboration with Abacus Evaluation presents this 2‑hour online course that will include hands-on practice.

This course introduces participants to the use of logic models as practical tools for program evaluation.

Logic models provide a structured way to articulate program theory, clarify assumptions, and make explicit the pathways through which program inputs and activities or strategies are expected to lead to outcomes and impact. In this course, participants will learn the core components and types of logic models, examine real‑world examples, and practice developing logic models for a program or project. The course will also demonstrate how logic models can be used to guide decisions about what to measure and when.

This course is designed for anyone including researchers, program staff, and students who want a clear, systematic approach to evaluating programs and projects.

Registration and fee required to receive Zoom link access.

title: Fireside Chat with Jen Psaki
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Nelson Mandela Auditorium
description:
Join the UNC Hussman Political Communication Focus Program for a fireside chat featuring former White House press secretary Jen Psaki, moderated by Jennifer Davis, Knott Distinguished Professor of the Practice in the UNC Curriculum in Peace, War and Defense.

 

About Jen Psaki

Psaki is the anchor of MS NOW’s “The Briefing with Jen Psaki” and host of the MS NOW original podcast “The Blueprint with Jen Psaki.”

 

The former White House press secretary for President Joe Biden was lauded by the Associated Press as a communicator who “dug deep into policy, seeking an understanding that goes far beyond talking points,” and was celebrated for bringing “a mixture of warmth, humor, intelligence and edge” to her role by Vogue.

 

Prior to her time in the Biden White House, Psaki was a longtime adviser to President Barack Obama and served as a traveling press secretary on his first long-shot campaign, and later served as the White House communications director.

 

Additionally, Psaki also served as the administration’s public face on the global stage during her tenure as the State Department spokesperson, traveling the world with Secretary of State John Kerry. Psaki is also the author of “Say More: Lessons from Work, the White House, and the World” (Scribner, 2024).

 

Psaki graduated from the College of William & Mary with a double major in English and sociology. While at William & Mary, she was a member of the swim team, Chi Omega sorority and was involved in several other campus programs and activities. 

 

---

 

This event is hosted by the UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media and is open to the Carolina community. UNC students seeking CLE credit can register on Heel Life. Pre-registration is not required for other attendees.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: On the Rocks: A Scree & Crevice Garden Tour
location: Duke Gardens–Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
At first glance, a pile of rocks seems like the last place a plant would want to call home—yet the scree and crevice gardens at Duke Gardens are bursting with an array of tenacious, beautiful and cleverly adapted plants. Join Branden Kowalyszyn, horticulturist of the Gateway Gardens at Duke Gardens, for a guided tour through these rugged landscapes, where sharp drainage, shifting gravel and thin soils support an extraordinary community of plants from around the world. Explore the artistry and science that goes into creating these gardens, including how the angle of a tilted stone, the chemistry of the gravel and the geometry of a crevice allow these plants to live here. Learn how a plant’s form, texture and growth habit reveal its survival strategies. Whether you’re a seasoned gardener looking for new ideas or someone who has walked past a rock garden and wondered what’s going on, you’ll get an insider’s look at the horticultural craft required to create these habitats and leave with an appreciation for plants’ ability to thrive even in the hardest of places. 
Fee: $24; free for Duke Gardens members with discount code. 
Parking: Parking fees apply. 
Location: Meet at the Barnes Welcome Center. 
Accessibility: This will be a small group program that takes place outdoors, traveling on a combination of paved and unpaved paths with some uneven surfaces and moderate inclines.

This course offers an overview of how AI tools such as large language models (LLMS) can enhance early stages of the survey process, including item generation, questionnaire evaluation, and survey refinement. title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.
